about:
The MySQL privileges that make an account an administrator of the SERVER rather than a user of a database. Written here rather than in a rule for one reason above the others: `SUPER` was deprecated in 8.0 and its powers split across a family of dynamic privileges, so a check that looks only for `SUPER` comes back empty on a correctly configured 8.4 server whose account is administrator in every way that matters. A list in code is a list nobody reconciles against the server; a list here carries its reason and is reconciled by a test that asks the server to accept every name. That reconciliation earned itself immediately: the first version of this file carried `SET_USER_ID`, which MySQL 8.4 refuses outright — it was split into SET_ANY_DEFINER and ALLOW_NONEXISTENT_DEFINER, and a rule reading the old name would have matched nothing on the engine this package targets while looking exactly like a rule with nothing to report.

RECONCILED IN BOTH DIRECTIONS SINCE 2026-09-20. The arm that asks the server to accept every listed name proves VALIDITY and, by construction, can never find something MISSING — and 40 administrative privileges were missing, among them BINLOG_ADMIN, BACKUP_ADMIN, CLONE_ADMIN and the whole replication family the rule's own docblock names as its scope. A second arm now diffs the other way, and it takes the scope from the SERVER rather than from a judgment: every privilege MySQL reports with `Context = 'Server Admin'` must be either an entry here or a declared exclusion in `excluded`, each with its reason. A privilege that is neither is red. The `excluded` list is short and each line says why, because an exclusion without a reason is how a list starts drifting again.

entries.grants: Creating an object whose DEFINER does not exist, which defers the question of whose privileges it runs with until somebody creates that account. The other half of the old SET_USER_ID.
Managing an account's secondary password, the mechanism that lets a credential be rotated while both are accepted.
Exemption from an audit rule that would otherwise abort the connection, so this account keeps working where policy says it should not.
Configuring the audit log, including what is recorded and what is not.
Changing the server's authentication policy, which decides which factors and plugins an account may use.
Backup operations, including LOCK INSTANCE FOR BACKUP — which blocks every DDL on the instance for as long as it is held, so this privilege can stop a deployment.
Control over the binary log itself: purging it and changing how it is written. The binary log is how replicas and point-in-time recovery see history, so this reaches durability beyond this server.
Turning binary-log and relay-log encryption on or off, which decides whether that history is written in the clear.
Cloning: provisioning this server from another, or serving as the donor. A clone REPLACES the recipient data directory.
Killing other accounts' sessions and connecting past max_connections and read_only — the ability to act on other users' work.
Creating roles, which are accounts that grant privileges to other accounts.
Creating, altering and dropping tablespaces, which decides where data files live on the server's filesystem.
Creating, dropping, renaming and re-authenticating ANY account on the server. An account with it can mint itself a second account, which makes every other restriction on the first one provisional.
Dropping roles, which removes whatever they granted from every account that held them.
Rotating the InnoDB master encryption key, on which the readability of every encrypted tablespace depends.

Reading and writing files anywhere the server process can, as the server process — LOAD DATA INFILE and SELECT … INTO OUTFILE. The sharpest of the static ones: it turns database access into filesystem access on the database host, and it is the privilege an import tool asks for once and nobody narrows afterwards.
Exemption from firewall restrictions, so statements another account would be refused are allowed for this one.
FLUSH OPTIMIZER_COSTS, which reloads the cost constants the optimizer plans with.
FLUSH PRIVILEGES, which reloads the grant tables — the step that makes a hand-edited grant table take effect.
FLUSH STATUS, which resets the counters other tooling reads to judge the server.
FLUSH TABLES, including WITH READ LOCK, which makes the whole server read-only for as long as it is held.
FLUSH USER_RESOURCES, which resets per-account resource counters.

Handing privileges on. Listed so the vocabulary is complete and marked unjudged here on purpose: it is a property OF a grant rather than an administrative power over the server, and it has its own rule. Two rules about one fact is the double report this catalog refuses.
Starting and stopping Group Replication and changing its membership, which decides which servers hold the group.
Acting as a Group Replication stream connection, the channel members use to exchange state.
Starting and stopping redo-log archiving, which writes the redo stream to a path this privilege names.
Disabling and re-enabling the InnoDB redo log. With it off the server is not crash-safe.
Running OPTIMIZE TABLE on the local server, which rebuilds a table and can hold it for the duration.
Administering accounts that authenticate without a password.
Persisting read-only variables, so a change survives a restart — the difference between altering the server now and altering it permanently.

Seeing every session's currently executing statement, across all accounts. A statement is where credentials and personal data pass through in the clear, so this reads other tenants' traffic without touching their tables.
FLUSH of logs, caches, privileges and tables, plus RESET. It reaches the server's own bookkeeping, including re-reading the grant tables and taking a global read lock.
Asking about replication position and topology.
Reading binary log events from this server, which is the whole write history of every database on it.
Acting as the applier thread: executing changes as the replication channel does, including with binary logging suppressed.
Starting, stopping and reconfiguring replication on this server, including where it replicates from.
Creating and altering resource groups and moving other sessions between them, which decides what CPU other work gets.
Granting and revoking roles with WITH ADMIN OPTION, which reaches every privilege any role carries.
Reading system variables the server otherwise hides, which are hidden because their values are secrets.
Connecting on the administrative interface, which is reachable when the ordinary connection limit is exhausted.
Setting restricted session variables — including the ones that disable checks the server otherwise enforces on this connection.
Setting a routine, view or trigger DEFINER to another account — the ability to have the server run code as somebody else. It is one half of what SET_USER_ID used to cover.
Reading the definition of every stored routine on the server, including ones this account cannot execute.
Stopping the server. Not a data privilege in any sense, and an application account holding it hands availability to whoever holds the credential.
Nearly every administrative action at once: killing other sessions, changing global variables, bypassing read_only, setting a routine's DEFINER to another account.
Marking an account as a system account — and, more importantly here, the power to modify system accounts, which accounts without it cannot touch.
Changing any global system variable, which reaches the server's durability, replication and security settings alike.
Overriding the default encryption rules a schema or the server sets, so a table can be created unencrypted where policy says otherwise.
Administering the telemetry log.
Setting a tag on a transaction GTID, which labels entries in the replication history other servers apply.
XA RECOVER, which lists prepared transactions left by other sessions so they can be committed or rolled back.

excluded.reason: Creating and running scheduled events is schema-level work an application account may legitimately need; the server files it under Server Admin because the scheduler is server-wide, not because the privilege administers the server.

Administrative in substance — it lets an account connect AS another — but it is not a global privilege: the syntax is GRANT PROXY ON 'user'@'host', never ON *.*, so it cannot be named in the shape the rules reading this list match. Excluded rather than listed because the reconciliation arm proved the point: the server refused GRANT PROXY ON *.* with error 1064. It needs its own check, not an entry here.
Lets an account move its OWN thread between resource groups. The administrative counterpart, RESOURCE_GROUP_ADMIN, is listed; this one cannot affect anybody else.

An 8.0 name that MySQL 8.4 refuses outright: it was split into SET_ANY_DEFINER and ALLOW_NONEXISTENT_DEFINER, and both of those ARE listed. Named here so a run against a sub-floor 8.0 server does not report it as an omission.
Lets an account SEE schema names it has no rights in. That is a disclosure concern and not control over the server, and the rules this list feeds are about administrative power.
MySQL's placeholder for no privileges at all. Every account has it, so treating it as administrative would make every account an administrator.
